Something is indeterminable when it is impossible — or at least practically impossible — to figure out, measure, calculate, or settle with certainty. The word describes a situation where a clear, definite answer simply cannot be reached, no matter how hard you try or how many tools and methods you use.

There is a crucial difference between something that hasn't been determined yet and something that cannot be determined at all. "Indeterminable" belongs to the second category — it signals impossibility, not just incompleteness.

  • "The cause of the fire is undetermined" → investigators are still working; an answer may come.
  • "The cause of the fire is indeterminable" → all investigation has been exhausted, or the means to find an answer simply don't exist; no answer is reachable.

This makes "indeterminable" a stronger, more final word than most of its cousins.
What kinds of things get called "indeterminable"?
1. When something cannot be measured or calculated

The exact age of an unidentified fossil may be indeterminable if none of the usual dating methods can be applied. The temperature at the core of a distant star might be indeterminable with current instruments.
2. When a question cannot be answered with certainty
The exact number of words Shakespeare spoke in his lifetime is indeterminable — there are no records, no way to even estimate reliably, and no future discovery could ever settle it.
3. When a dispute or problem cannot be resolved

A philosophical debate about what existed before the universe may be indeterminable because it lies entirely outside the reach of observation or logic.

4. When the extent or limit of something cannot be perceived or measured
Writers sometimes use the word to describe something that seems boundless: "an indeterminable stretch of darkness," meaning you cannot tell where it ends. This sense is less common but perfectly valid.
How it differs from closely related words

Understanding a word gets much sharper when you see how it stands apart from its neighbors:

  • Indeterminate — This is the closest relative and often confused with "indeterminable." "Indeterminate" tends to mean not clearly defined or not yet settled, and it's common in technical fields (mathematics, law, biology). An indeterminate prison sentence is one with no fixed end date — but it could be decided later. "Indeterminable" leans more toward impossible to determine, making it the harder, more absolute of the two.
  • Undetermined — Simply means "not yet figured out." It leaves the door open. Something undetermined today might be determined tomorrow. "Indeterminable" closes that door.
  • Inconclusive — Describes evidence or results that don't point to a clear answer. The test results were inconclusive. Notice that "inconclusive" describes the evidence, while "indeterminable" describes the thing itself.
  • Unknowable — This is more philosophical and total: something unknowable can never be known by anyone, ever, by the very nature of what it is. "Indeterminable" is more practical and contextual — it often means we lack the tools, data, or access, not necessarily that the answer doesn't exist somewhere in principle.
  • Immeasurable — Specifically about size or quantity; often used positively ("immeasurable kindness"). "Indeterminable" is broader and more neutral.
  • Indefinite — Means vague, not clearly defined, or open-ended. An indefinite delay could end at any moment. It has a softer, more temporary feeling than "indeterminable."

"Indeterminable" is a formal word. You won't often hear it in everyday casual conversation. You're most likely to encounter it in:

  • Scientific writing: "The exact mutation rate is indeterminable at this stage."
  • Legal or forensic contexts: "The time of death was indeterminable."
  • Philosophy: "Whether free will exists may be indeterminable by rational argument alone."
  • Literature: Authors use it to evoke vastness, mystery, or hopelessness.

In everyday speech, people would more naturally say "we can't figure it out," "there's no way to know," or "it's impossible to say." "Indeterminable" is the formal, precise version of those ideas.

• "After years of study, the precise authorship of the manuscript remained indeterminable." (No definitive answer is possible.)
  • "The depth of her grief was indeterminable — it seemed to have no bottom." (Its extent cannot be measured.)
  • "Whether the ancient civilization collapsed due to drought or disease is largely indeterminable from the artifacts alone." (The evidence can't take us to a certain conclusion.)
  • "The question of what moral goodness really is may be philosophically indeterminable." (It resists any definitive resolution.)

Indeterminable means impossible to determine — it describes something that cannot be figured out, measured, or resolved with certainty, not because no one has tried, but because the means to reach a definite answer are unavailable or the question is inherently beyond resolution.
